items.prompt: An undirected graph contains the cycle 0—1—2—0. A traversal starts at 0 and must process each vertex once. Which visited-state rule is sufficient for ordinary reachability traversal?

options.text: Use no visited state because every traversal creates a tree before it follows any edge.
Use an adjacency matrix; matrix storage prevents repeated visits automatically.
When a vertex is first accepted into the traversal frontier, mark it discovered; expand only discovered vertices that have not yet been processed.
Mark a vertex only after recursively exploring every neighbor, with no active-state guard.

feedback.reason: Cycle safety comes from recording discovery before another path can schedule the same state.

blocks.text: Claim a vertex before following its edges

items: Accept 0 into the frontier and mark 0 discovered.
When 1 is first reached, mark it before expanding its neighbors; do the same for 2.
When edge 2—0 is inspected, 0 is already discovered, so no new frontier entry or recursive call is created.
The traversal finishes after processing each of 0, 1, and 2 once.

blocks.text: Marking only after all neighbors finish would allow the active chain 0 → 1 → 2 to enter 0 again before any call is complete. A matrix records the cycle edge but not whether this traversal already claimed its endpoint.

blocks.title: Discovery invariant
blocks.text: Mark at frontier acceptance so every graph vertex is scheduled at most once.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_visited_tree: The traversal tree is a result of selecting discovery edges; the input still contains non-tree edges that can lead back to an earlier vertex.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.mark_after_all_neighbors: On the cycle, 0 can call 1, 1 can call 2, and 2 can call 0 before any call is marked complete.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_prevents_cycle: A representation records edges but does not record which states this traversal has already discovered.

items.prompt: Order the discovery-state actions for considering neighbor v from a dequeued BFS vertex u so that v is scheduled at most once.

elements.text: Test whether v is still unseen.
Record any discovery metadata, such as parent or distance.

feedback.reason: The unseen test and discovery mark must precede publication of v to the queue.

blocks.text: Publish one fully initialized frontier entry

items: Test whether v is unseen.
Mark v discovered so later predecessors cannot claim it.
Record parent[v] = u, distance[v], or other first-discovery metadata.
Enqueue the already-claimed and initialized v.

blocks.text: Once v is visible in the queue, another vertex may be processed before v is dequeued. Publishing first and marking later would let that predecessor enqueue a duplicate; recording metadata later could also separate v from the discovery event that owns its parent and distance.

blocks.title: Atomic logical event
blocks.text: Test, claim, initialize, then enqueue.

items.prompt: Recursive DFS explores an undirected graph. When processing edge u—v, v is already visited. What may be concluded from that fact alone?
constraints: The graph is simple: it has no self-loops or parallel edges.

options.text: Every edge to a visited vertex proves a cycle.
Nothing about a cycle yet; v may be u's parent, so parent or equivalent context is needed.
A visited neighbor can never participate in a cycle because DFS already chose a tree edge.
Only BFS can classify this case because BFS is always faster than DFS.

feedback.reason: In an undirected graph, the parent edge returns to an already visited vertex without forming a new cycle witness.

blocks.text: A visited parent is expected in an undirected adjacency list

items: If DFS reached u through tree edge v—u, then u's adjacency list naturally contains the reverse view u—v.
Seeing that visited parent v does not add a second route; it is the same simple undirected edge.
If visited v is not u's parent, the DFS tree path between u and v plus edge u—v forms a cycle.

blocks.text: Thus `visited(v)` alone is insufficient: the algorithm must compare v with parent[u]. The simple-graph constraint matters; with parallel edges, edge identity rather than only parent vertex identity is needed to distinguish the tree edge from a second edge.

blocks.title: Undirected rule
blocks.text: A visited non-parent neighbor proves a cycle in a simple undirected graph.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.cycle_always: The reverse representation of the tree edge to u's parent is expected in an undirected adjacency list.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_cycle_ever: An edge to a visited non-parent vertex is precisely the relevant undirected-cycle signal.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_only: Traversal speed is not the classification rule; DFS with parent context can detect this condition correctly.

items.prompt: A directed graph must be checked for a cycle with DFS. Why is one boolean visited flag per vertex insufficient for interpreting an edge u → v?

options.text: Because directed graphs are trees when traversed recursively, so no state is needed.
Because every edge to any visited vertex is automatically a directed cycle.
Because only adjacency matrices can store the required DFS colors.
Because visited must be refined into at least active-on-current-path versus fully finished state.

feedback.reason: A directed back edge is an edge to a vertex still active on the current DFS path, not merely any previously visited vertex.

blocks.text: Directed cycle evidence depends on the current DFS path

items: An unseen vertex has not entered DFS.
On entry, mark it active while its recursive frame remains on the current path.
After all outgoing edges finish, change it from active to finished.
An edge u → v closes a directed cycle exactly when v is active; an edge to finished v does not return to the current path.

blocks.text: One boolean merges active and finished vertices and therefore cannot distinguish a back edge from a cross or forward edge. These colors are traversal metadata and work with lists, matrices, or implicit neighbors.

blocks.title: Three-state rule
blocks.text: Use unseen, active, and finished; only an edge to active state is a directed DFS cycle witness.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.visited_never_needed: Directed graphs can contain cycles and converging paths; recursion does not remove them.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.every_visited_cycle: An edge to a fully finished vertex may be a cross or forward edge and need not close the current recursion path.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_colors: DFS colors are traversal metadata independent of whether edges are stored in lists, matrices, or generated implicitly.

items.prompt: In BFS, source s has edges to a and b, and both a and b have an edge to c. c is initially unseen. What operational difference arises if c is marked visited only when dequeued, with no separate queued-state check?

options.text: The second copy gives c a shorter distance than the first.
Both a and b can enqueue c, creating duplicate frontier entries before the first copy is dequeued.
c will never be processed because dequeue marking suppresses both copies.
The queue silently becomes a DFS stack when duplicate entries exist.

feedback.reason: Until the first copy is dequeued, every predecessor still observes c as unseen.

blocks.text: The pending copy is invisible to a visited-on-dequeue rule

items: Processing s enqueues a and b.
Processing a sees unseen c and enqueues one copy, but c remains unmarked.
Before that copy reaches the front, b is processed and also sees c as unseen.
b enqueues a second copy of c.

blocks.text: Both copies have the same candidate distance because a and b are in the same BFS layer. A dequeue-time implementation can skip stale copies with an additional processed guard, but it has already lost the one-enqueue-per-vertex space and work bound. Expanding duplicates can multiply later work further.

blocks.title: Timing rule
blocks.text: Mark on enqueue to make pending discovery visible to every later predecessor.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.shorter_distance: Both copies are generated from the same BFS layer, so they imply the same candidate distance.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.missed_vertex: At least the first dequeued copy can still be processed; the issue is duplicate scheduling, not guaranteed omission.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.dfs_conversion: Duplicate entries do not change FIFO into LIFO; they change work and memory behavior.

items.prompt: A maze state includes the current cell and a bitmask of collected keys. Reaching cell x with keymask 001 and later reaching x with keymask 101 can enable different future moves. What should the visited identity be?

options.text: The cell only; a vertex may never be visited twice in any graph traversal.
The keymask only; location is merely representation detail.
The pair (cell, keymask), because future legal transitions depend on both components.
No visited state, because a grid is a tree when obstacles are fixed.

feedback.reason: Visited identity must contain every variable that changes the set or cost of future transitions.

blocks.text: Visited identity must predict future behavior

items: State (x, 001) means the traversal is at x with only the key encoded by bit 001.
State (x, 101) is at the same cell but has an additional key, so a locked outgoing move may be legal only from this state.
Collapsing both into visited[x] can discard the second arrival and incorrectly report a reachable target as unreachable.

blocks.text: The correct vertex identity is therefore (cell, keymask). Cell alone loses capability; keymask alone loses location. The same rule applies to remaining obstacle removals, direction, fuel, turn count, or any history variable that changes future legal moves or costs.

blocks.title: State-design rule
blocks.text: Two arrivals may share one physical object yet be different graph vertices when their future transitions differ.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.cell_only: These are distinct search states even though they share a physical coordinate; collapsing them can discard a solvable route.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.keys_only: Legal next moves also depend on the current cell, so keymask alone merges unrelated states.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.no_visited: Grid movement commonly permits cycles, and the augmented state graph can revisit coordinates under different key sets.

items.prompt: The same immutable graph receives two independent reachability queries with different sources. How should ordinary visited state be scoped?

options.text: Keep vertices permanently visited after the first query so later traversals are faster.
Store visited flags inside the adjacency list as part of the graph's permanent representation.
BFS may reuse permanent visited state because it is always faster than DFS.
Use fresh logical visited state per query, possibly implemented with a query-generation stamp.

feedback.reason: Visited means discovered in this traversal, not globally exhausted for all future questions.

blocks.text: Visited answers “discovered by which traversal?”

items: A fresh boolean array gives the second query a logically empty discovered set.
A generation-stamp array can avoid O(V) clearing: a vertex is visited for query q only when stamp[v] = q.
Reusing the first query's marks without a query identity can suppress vertices that the second source must explore.

blocks.text: Adjacency is immutable graph data; visited is execution state. Reusable preprocessing must compute a different durable answer structure—for example, component labels for repeated connectivity queries in an undirected graph—rather than treating one source's traversal marks as universal.

blocks.title: Scope rule
blocks.text: Keep visited logically per query even when generation stamps reuse the same physical array.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.permanent: A vertex reached from the first source may still need to be explored to answer a later query; permanent marks change the second query's semantics.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.representation_owned: Visited state belongs to one traversal execution, while adjacency is static input structure.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.bfs_global: Neither traversal order authorizes carrying state across logically independent queries.

items.prompt: Select all statements that correctly separate tree traversal state from general graph traversal state.

options.text: An adjacency matrix makes a discovered set unnecessary because repeated edges occupy the same cell.
In a guaranteed undirected tree, carrying the parent can prevent immediately traversing the same edge backward.
The parent-only rule applies unchanged to every graph, including graphs with longer cycles.
In a general graph, a discovered set is needed because a vertex may be reached through non-parent edges.

feedback.reason: A tree's structural promise can reduce traversal state; a general graph has no such promise.

blocks.text: Structural promises determine the minimum traversal state

items: In a guaranteed undirected tree, every two vertices have one simple path. Passing parent lets a child skip the reverse view of its tree edge, and no longer cycle exists.
In a general graph, a non-parent edge can return to an ancestor or converge on a vertex discovered by another branch, so a global per-traversal discovered set is required.
An adjacency matrix changes how edges are enumerated but does not record which traversal paths have already reached a vertex.

blocks.text: The parent-only rule is safe because the input contract proves acyclicity and unique paths, not because recursion creates a tree. Applying it to a cyclic graph can revisit an ancestor without using the immediate parent edge.

blocks.title: Transfer rule
blocks.text: Use parent-only traversal state only under a proven tree contract; otherwise track discovery globally for the traversal.

wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.tree_rule_general: A cycle can return to an ancestor or reach a previously explored branch without using the immediate parent edge.
wrongOptionExplanationsByOptionId.matrix_is_visited: Edge storage deduplicates an edge representation, not traversal arrivals through different paths.

omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.tree_parent_may_suffice: The guaranteed tree structure removes all cycles except the immediate representation of the parent edge.
omittedCorrectExplanationsByOptionId.graph_needs_discovered: General graphs permit converging paths and cycles, so parent context alone cannot identify every prior discovery.
